Correlations Adjusted for Common Method Variance, With Intervals and Tests

Source: R/common_method_adjusted_r.R
common_method_adjusted_r.Rd

When every variable in a study is measured the same way, often by one respondent on one questionnaire, part of each correlation can come from the shared method rather than from the constructs. The marker variable technique of Lindell and Whitney (2001) takes a correlation that should be zero on substantive grounds, the correlation \(r_M\) of a marker variable with the substantive variables, as an estimate of the method effect common to every correlation, and removes it from each substantive correlation. common_method_adjusted_r() returns, for one or more values of \(r_M\), every adjusted correlation with its confidence interval and Lindell and Whitney's t test, so that a reader can see whether a relationship survives the adjustment and how that conclusion depends on the marker correlation assumed.

The marker correlation is itself an estimate, and the proxy used when no marker was measured (the smallest positive correlation among the substantive variables) is a choice. Reading the adjusted correlations over a grid of values of \(r_M\), from no adjustment to a generous one, is the treatment of that uncertainty: a correlation whose interval excludes zero across the plausible range does not depend on the value chosen. common_method_marker reports the adjusted matrix for a single marker correlation without intervals or tests, since it does not take \(N\); this function takes \(N\) and gives both.

Usage

common_method_adjusted_r(R, N, marker_r = NULL, conf_level = 0.95)

# S3 method for class 'dmar_common_method_adjusted_r'
tidy(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'dmar_common_method_adjusted_r'
glance(x, ...)

Arguments

R

A correlation matrix among the substantive variables (not the marker): symmetric, with a unit diagonal. Its column (or row) names name the variables; an unnamed matrix gets V1, V2, and so on.

N

The sample size on which R rests, at least 4.

marker_r

One or more marker correlations \(r_M\), each in \((-1, 1)\), in the order the rows should follow. When NULL (the default) the smallest positive off-diagonal correlation in R is used as the proxy marker, as in common_method_marker.

conf_level

Confidence level of the intervals (default 0.95).

x

A dmar_common_method_adjusted_r table returned by common_method_adjusted_r().

...

Unused.

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_tbl) with one row per value of marker_r and pair of variables, the pairs in the order (1, 2), (1, 3), ..., (2, 3), ... within each marker value, and the columns marker_r, variable_1, variable_2, r (the unadjusted correlation), estimate (the adjusted correlation), ci_lower, ci_upper, t_value, df (\(N - 3\)), and p_value. The attributes are adjusted (a list of the adjusted correlation matrices, one per value of marker_r, named by it), N, conf_level, and marker_rule ("smallest_positive" when the proxy was used, "supplied" otherwise). tidy() returns one row per pair and marker value, with term naming the pair ("variable_1:variable_2") and the columns marker_r, r, estimate, ci_lower, ci_upper, statistic (the t), df, p_value, and conf_level; glance() returns n_pairs, n_markers, N, and conf_level.

Details

The adjustment. Each substantive correlation \(r_{ij}\) is adjusted as $$r^{A}_{ij} = \frac{r_{ij} - r_M}{1 - r_M}$$ (Lindell & Whitney, 2001, Equation 4), the partial correlation of \(i\) and \(j\) with the method effect removed when that effect contributes the same \(r_M\) to every correlation. The adjusted matrix for each value of marker_r is the "adjusted" attribute; for a single value it equals the "adjusted" attribute of common_method_marker.

The test. Lindell and Whitney (2001, Equation 5) test each adjusted correlation as a partial correlation with one variable partialed out, $$t = \frac{r^{A}}{\sqrt{(1 - (r^{A})^2) / (N - 3)}},$$ referred to the t distribution with \(N - 3\) degrees of freedom, with a two-sided p-value.

The interval. With \(r_M\) treated as known, the adjustment is an increasing linear function of the population correlation \(\rho_{ij}\), so a confidence interval for \(\rho_{ij}\) maps into one for the adjusted correlation with the same coverage: each limit of the Fisher's Z interval for \(\rho_{ij}\) (the interval of ci_r, based on the variance \(1/(N - 3)\)) is adjusted by the same equation as the correlation. A lower limit that the map carries below \(-1\) is set to \(-1\), the bound of a correlation. Because the map is increasing, that happens exactly when the lower limit for \(\rho_{ij}\) falls below \(2 r_M - 1\), whatever the sign of \(r_{ij}\) or of the adjusted correlation: never when \(r_M \le 0\); for \(0 < r_M < .5\) only when the lower limit for \(\rho_{ij}\) is negative, as it is for a negative correlation, one near zero, or one from a small sample (with \(r_{ij} = .35\), \(N = 5\), and \(r_M = .3\) the adjusted correlation is .071 and its lower limit is set to \(-1\)); and for \(r_M \ge .5\) even when that limit is positive. The interval is conditional on \(r_M\): it carries the sampling variability of \(r_{ij}\) and none of that of the marker correlation, which is what the grid over marker_r is for.

An adjusted correlation at or beyond \(\pm 1\) lies outside the range of a correlation. It arises from a correlation below \(2 r_M - 1\), which a method effect of \(r_M\) common to every correlation cannot produce (or from a correlation of exactly 1), and it gets no interval and no test: its ci_lower, ci_upper, t_value, and p_value are NA.

The interval and the test are different approximations. The interval excludes zero exactly when the Fisher's Z interval for \(\rho_{ij}\) excludes \(r_M\), while the test treats the adjusted correlation as a sample partial correlation, so near the boundary of significance the two can disagree. The test is kept for parity with the paper; the interval is what to report beside the estimate. Neither is adjusted for the number of pairs or of marker values.

Reading the results. The proxy marker is one of the substantive correlations, so the pair that supplied it is adjusted to exactly zero and its test says nothing about that pair. The technique presumes the variables are reflected so that their intercorrelations are positive; a negative correlation is pushed further from zero rather than toward it, so reverse code as needed before computing R. A correlation that remains different from zero after the adjustment is consistent with a relationship that is not only a method artifact, under the assumption that the method effect is the same for every pair; it is not evidence that no method variance is present.

References

Lindell, M. K., & Whitney, D. J. (2001). Accounting for common method variance in cross-sectional research designs. Journal of Applied Psychology, 86(1), 114–121. doi:10.1037/0021-9010.86.1.114

See also

common_method_marker for the adjusted matrix and its summary at one marker correlation; common_method_single_factor for the single-factor screen; ci_r for the interval of an unadjusted correlation.

Examples

# Visual, textual, and speed composites of the nine Holzinger and
# Swineford tests in the primary set, each the mean of three tests.
hs <- holzinger_swineford
scores <- data.frame(
  visual  = rowMeans(hs[c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes",
                          "t4_lozenges")]),
  textual = rowMeans(hs[c("t6_paragraph_comprehension", "t7_sentence",
                          "t9_word_meaning")]),
  speed   = rowMeans(hs[c("t10_addition", "t12_counting_groups_of_dots",
                          "t13_straight_and_curved_capitals")]))
R <- stats::cor(scores)

# The smallest positive correlation as the proxy marker; the pair that
# supplied it (textual with speed) is adjusted to zero. Visual with
# speed shows the interval and the test parting near the boundary: the
# interval includes zero while the p-value is below .05.
common_method_adjusted_r(R, N = nrow(scores))
#>  marker_r variable_1 variable_2 r     estimate ci_lower ci_upper t_value df 
#>  0.237    visual     textual    0.312 0.098    -0.041   0.227    1.700   298
#>  0.237    visual     speed      0.326 0.116    -0.021   0.244    2.022   298
#>  0.237    textual    speed      0.237 0.000    -0.144   0.136    0.000   298
#>  p_value
#>  0.0901 
#>  0.0440 
#>  1.0000 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# A grid of marker correlations, from no adjustment to a large one.
grid <- common_method_adjusted_r(R, N = nrow(scores),
                                 marker_r = c(0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3))
grid[grid$variable_1 == "visual" & grid$variable_2 == "textual", ]
#>  marker_r variable_1 variable_2 r     estimate ci_lower ci_upper t_value df 
#>  0.000    visual     textual    0.312 0.312    0.206    0.411    5.670   298
#>  0.100    visual     textual    0.312 0.236    0.118    0.345    4.185   298
#>  0.200    visual     textual    0.312 0.140    0.008    0.263    2.442   298
#>  0.300    visual     textual    0.312 0.017    -0.134   0.158    0.298   298
#>  p_value 
#>  < 0.0001
#>  < 0.0001
#>  0.0152  
#>  0.7662  
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
attr(grid, "adjusted")[["0.2"]]
#>            visual   textual     speed
#> visual  1.0000000 0.1400825 0.1575495
#> textual 0.1400825 1.0000000 0.0466276
#> speed   0.1575495 0.0466276 1.0000000
